metric: temperature window of rapid oil removal increase and onset of Fucus thermal injury/mortality
reported_effect: Oil removal increased most rapidly between 40 C and 60 C and between 18.6 and 60 kPa (2.7-8.7 psi); Fucus color change/mucus began at 40 C and significant mortality occurred between 40 C and 80 C

notes: Demonstrates that temperature levels where heated low-pressure flushing becomes effective at removing Bunker C (40-60 C) coincide with the thermal threshold for acute injury and mortality in Fucus gardneri (>=40 C).

metric: contact water pressure causing frond tearing and statistically significant mortality

design: controlled factorial field experiment on intertidal plots (reported in NOAA synthesis)

location: Pacific Northwest / British Columbia intertidal test bed

notes: 344.1 kPa (50 psi) at 15.2 cm from the substrate corresponds to the lower boundary of high-pressure washing in Owens et al. (2021) Table 4 (350-7000 kPa / 50-1000 psi).

treatment_detail: Synthesis of worldwide rocky shore cleanup operations (high-pressure washing, hot-water washing, dispersants) vs untreated natural clearance
metric: time to ecological recovery of shore biota
reported_effect: Ecological recovery of rocky shore biota usually takes up to 3 years (and salt marshes up to 5 years) regardless of cleanup; cleanup has a negative or marginal influence on recovery time except for thick smothering or toxic subsurface deposits
design: systematic literature synthesis of field spills and experimental clearances
spill_or_experiment: AURIS worldwide synthesis of rocky shore and salt marsh oil spills and experimental clearances
citation: Sell D, Conway L, Clark T, Picken GB, Baker JM, Dunnet GM, McIntyre AD, Clark RB (1995) Scientific criteria to optimize oil spill cleanup. International Oil Spill Conference Proceedings 1995(1):595-600.
notes: Global synthesis concluding that shoreline washing/cleanup on rocky shores has a negative or marginal effect on ecological recovery timescales (typically <=3 yr).

habitat: salt marsh tidal mesocosm (Spartina alterniflora, mudflat sediment, and ceramic seawall tiles)

treatment_detail: PES-51 (~192 mL/mesocosm sprayed on oiled tiles, 30-min soak, 1 L/side seawater rinse) vs Oiled seawater-rinsed control
outcome: infauna survival (polychaete Neanthes arenaceodentata and amphipod Leptocheirus plumulosus)
metric: polychaete 14-d survival
design: replicated tidal salt-marsh mesocosm experiment with untreated oiled control and unoiled control
assignment: randomised mesocosm tanks (4 replicates per treatment)
spill_or_experiment: NOAA NCCOS salt marsh mesocosm study (DeLorenzo et al. 2017)
citation: DeLorenzo ME et al. (2017) NOAA Tech. Memo. NOS NCCOS 232.

Clam 30-d survival was 90-100% and mud snail 30-d survival was 74-85% in both Oil+PES-51 and Oil-alone.

spill_or_experiment: Prestige oil spill pilot rocky-shore CytoSol trial (Rial et al. 2010)

citation: Pezeshki SR, DeLaune RD, Jugsujinda A, Canevari GP, Lessard RR (1997) Major field test evaluates a shoreline cleaner to save oiled marsh grass. International Oil Spill Conference Proceedings 1997(1):397-402.

notes: Demonstrated short-term gas-exchange and shoot-count benefit when Corexit 9580 was applied 2 days after South Louisiana crude oiling, though 1-year biomass converged across oiled and oiled+cleaned treatments.
